subsection: 6. Direct Rule and the search for a settlement, 1974–1993

notes.h: Direct Rule after 1974: who governed and how
notes.b: After the power-sharing executive fell in 1974, Northern Ireland went back to being governed directly from London. This is the background to everything in this subsection, because no local government existed to solve the conflict.
points: Direct Rule (government of Northern Ireland straight from Westminster) was first imposed in March 1972, when the Stormont parliament was suspended. The power-sharing executive took office on 1 January 1974 and fell on 28 May 1974, so Direct Rule returned.

Under Direct Rule a Secretary of State and the Northern Ireland Office governed, which meant that decisions were made by British ministers rather than by elected local politicians, so local politicians had no real power.

The Secretaries of State were Merlyn Rees (1974 to 1976), Roy Mason (1976 to 1979), Humphrey Atkins (1979 to 1981), Jim Prior (1981 to 1984), Douglas Hurd (1984 to 1985), Tom King (1985 to 1989), Peter Brooke (1989 to 1992) and Patrick Mayhew (1992 to 1997).

Power sharing (unionists and nationalists sharing government) was the aim of most British and Irish policy after 1974, but it was not restored by 1993, so Direct Rule remained the basis of British policy throughout.
The Troubles began in 1969, and the Provisional IRA, loyalist paramilitaries and the British army were already in conflict when Direct Rule returned in 1974.

Terrorism, as used in this topic, means violence against civilians and the state for political ends. It is used here of the IRA and loyalist paramilitaries, and the British response was a mixture of security measures and politics.

The consent principle, that Northern Ireland's status would not change without the consent of a majority of its people, was already stated in 1973. It is the thread that runs through every step to 1993.
notes.tip: Direct Rule dates are a common confusion. Remember March 1972 (first imposed) and May 1974 (restored), and do not mix Direct Rule up with the 1975 Convention and 1982 Assembly, which were attempts at devolution.

notes.h: The Constitutional Convention, Ulsterisation and criminalisation
notes.b: While London governed, it tried one more devolved solution and then changed its security policy. In 1976 these changes shifted who fought the conflict and how prisoners were treated.
points: The Constitutional Convention was elected on 1 May 1975 to find a devolved settlement (one where Northern Ireland has its own local government). The unionist coalition (UUUC) held a majority in it.

The unionist majority recommended a return to majority rule, which meant government by the largest community. Westminster rejected this because it lacked cross-community support, and the Convention was dissolved in March 1976.

Ulsterisation was the policy, under Roy Mason from 1976, of giving the RUC (the police) and the Ulster Defence Regiment, or UDR (a locally recruited army regiment), the lead in security in place of the British army. The aim was to reduce the army's role.
Criminalisation was the policy of treating paramilitary offenders as ordinary criminals, not as political prisoners, so that violence would lose any political status.
Special category status, which had given paramilitary prisoners some of the privileges of political prisoners, was ended on 1 March 1976 for prisoners convicted of offences from that date.

Diplock courts, in which a judge sits without a jury for scheduled (terrorist-related) offences, had been introduced in 1973. They were meant to avoid jury intimidation and were part of the same approach.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the dates. Special category status ended on 1 March 1976, and this is separate from the blanket and dirty protests and from the hunger strikes of 1980 and 1981 that followed.

notes.b: In August 1976 a shocking accident turned ordinary people on to the streets in protest at the violence. The Peace People became the best-known peace movement of the Troubles, though it did not last.
points: On 10 August 1976 three children were killed in Belfast when a car, driven by an IRA volunteer who had been shot dead by soldiers, crashed into them. This tragedy was the cause of the movement.

Betty Williams, a witness to the crash, and Mairead Corrigan, the children's aunt, founded the Peace People in August 1976 and led the first peace march. The journalist Ciaran McKeown was a third founder.

The movement was one of ordinary people who held large peace rallies in Belfast and across Northern Ireland. It appealed to both communities and called for an end to paramilitary violence on both sides.
Williams and Corrigan were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for 1976. The award was announced in 1977, so the prize should not be dated 1977.
Contemporaries praised the movement, but some republicans and loyalists dismissed it as naive. Its support faded after 1977 because the violence continued.
notes.tip: Get the dates right: the Nobel Peace Prize was for 1976 and announced in 1977. Give the cause, the founders, the aim, the prize and the reasons for decline, and avoid crowd figures.

notes.h: The H-Blocks, the blanket and dirty protests and the hunger strikes, 1976–1981
notes.b: When special category status ended, republican prisoners fought back with protests inside the Maze prison. The protests escalated step by step to the hunger strikes of 1980 and 1981, in which the government and the prisoners each refused to give way.
points: The H-Blocks were the H-shaped cell blocks of the Maze prison, also called Long Kesh. Republican prisoners there wanted political status, meaning treatment as prisoners of war or political prisoners rather than as ordinary criminals.
The blanket protest began in 1976, when prisoners refused to wear prison uniform and wore only blankets. In 1978 it escalated into the dirty protest.
The first hunger strike (a refusal to eat) began in October 1980 and ended on 18 December 1980.

The second hunger strike began on 1 March 1981 under Bobby Sands, to demand the restoration of political status. He was elected MP for Fermanagh and South Tyrone in April 1981 while on hunger strike, which gave the protest wide publicity.
Sands died on 5 May 1981 after 66 days. Nine further hunger strikers died between May and August 1981, including Francis Hughes, Patsy O'Hara and Kieran Doherty, making ten deaths in all.
Margaret Thatcher declared that 'crime is crime is crime; it is not political', so her government refused to concede political status.
The hunger strike ended on 3 October 1981 without formal political status. Concessions were made afterwards, including on clothing and remission (shortened sentences).
notes.tip: Questions on this topic ask for the sequence from the end of special category status in 1976 to Sands's death and election. Keep the order clear: blanket protest, dirty protest, hunger strike of 1980, hunger strike of 1981.

notes.h: Effects of the hunger strikes and Sinn Féin's electoral strategy, 1981–1983
notes.b: The hunger strikes changed republican tactics. The publicity and sympathy they created showed that republicans could win votes, so Sinn Féin began to contest elections alongside the IRA campaign.
points: The strikes brought wide sympathy and recruits to republicans, and they hardened attitudes on both sides. They were also a propaganda success (propaganda means messages used to shape opinion), because each death drew attention to the republican case.
In June 1981 two prisoners, including Kieran Doherty, were elected to the Dáil (the Irish parliament), which showed that there was a republican vote to be won.
Owen Carron, Sands's election agent, won the Fermanagh and South Tyrone by-election in August 1981 as an Anti H-Block candidate, so Sands's seat stayed in republican hands.

Sinn Féin adopted an electoral strategy in 1981, summed up in the phrase 'the Armalite and the ballot box', used by Danny Morrison at the party's Ard Fheis (annual conference) in October 1981. It meant seeking votes while the armed campaign went on.
In the October 1982 Northern Ireland Assembly election Sinn Féin won five seats. Gerry Adams was among those elected, but the members abstained, which means they refused to take part.

In June 1983 Gerry Adams won the West Belfast seat at Westminster, which Gerry Fitt had held since 1966. Sinn Féin members refused to take their seats there, so they abstained from Westminster as well.
The strategy was a deliberate move to build political support. Critics regarded it as a cover for continued IRA violence.
notes.tip: Be ready to explain why the strikes changed republican tactics. The answer is that Sands's election and the later wins showed the movement could win votes.

notes.b: Adams was the Sinn Féin leader who turned the party into an electoral force, and he became the main republican voice in dealings with the British and Irish governments.
points: Gerry Adams was born in 1948 in Belfast and grew up in a republican family in West Belfast.
He was interned (imprisoned without trial) in the early 1970s. In July 1972 he was released to take part in the secret talks between the Provisional IRA and William Whitelaw in London.
He was elected president of Sinn Féin in November 1983, a post he held until 2018, and he led the party's move into electoral politics.
He took part in talks with the SDLP's John Hume in 1988 and again from 1991 to 1993, so he helped to shape the search for a settlement.

In October 1988 the Home Secretary, Douglas Hurd, banned the broadcast of the voices of Sinn Féin spokespeople, including Adams, as a propaganda move. Broadcasters used actors' voices, and the ban ended in 1994.
He was shaped by events too. He was shot and wounded by loyalist gunmen in Belfast in March 1984, lost his Westminster seat to Joe Hendron of the SDLP in 1992, and regained it in 1997.

Contemporaries disagreed about him. Supporters regarded him as the political face of the republican movement, while critics, including unionists and many nationalists, regarded him as the political wing of the IRA.

Supporters credit him with leading republicans from armed struggle towards negotiation. Critics, including unionists, argued that he used Sinn Féin's electoral strategy to complement the IRA campaign, so that republicans kept both.
Adams has always denied membership of the IRA, though others have alleged it.
notes.tip: Marks go to what he did, with dates (president from November 1983, electoral strategy, Hume–Adams), and to how contemporaries and historians judged him. He won West Belfast in 1983 and abstained throughout.

notes.h: The New Ireland Forum and Thatcher's rejection of its options
notes.b: In 1983 the Dublin government tried to agree a common nationalist view of the future. Its report offered Britain three options, and Margaret Thatcher's blunt rejection of them in 1984 showed how far Britain was willing to go.
points: The New Ireland Forum was set up in 1983 by the Dublin government, under the Taoiseach Garret FitzGerald. It included Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael, Labour and the SDLP, while Sinn Féin was excluded.
The unionist parties declined to take part, which meant that its report reflected the views of nationalist parties and the Dublin government only, so unionists could reject it.

The Forum's report, published on 2 May 1984, set out three options, such as a unitary Irish state, a federal or confederal state, and joint authority by Britain and Ireland. It said that the unitary state was the preferred option.
At a press conference on 19 November 1984, Margaret Thatcher rejected all three options, saying 'Out, out, out'.
Her rejection marked the limits of British willingness to change Northern Ireland's constitutional position in the mid-1980s, though within a year she signed an agreement giving Dublin a role.
notes.tip: Keep three dates apart: the Forum report (2 May 1984), the Brighton bomb (12 October 1984) and Thatcher's rejection (19 November 1984). Weak answers get these wrong.

notes.b: While the Forum's report was being debated, the IRA struck at the British government itself. The attack showed the danger of the campaign and strengthened Thatcher's security-first approach.
points: On 12 October 1984 the IRA bombed the Grand Hotel in Brighton, where the Conservative Party conference was being held. The target was the British government.
Five people were killed in the bombing, and Margaret Thatcher escaped. The IRA said it would try again, so security remained her priority.
Patrick Magee was later convicted of planting the bomb, which shows the attack was planned in advance.
notes.tip: Give the date, the target (the Conservative conference at the Grand Hotel), the five deaths, Thatcher's escape and Patrick Magee. Do not date it after Thatcher's Forum rejection.

notes.b: Thatcher was the British Prime Minister who led the government through the hunger strikes and signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement, a shift in British policy.
points: Margaret Thatcher was Prime Minister from May 1979 to November 1990, and she made security and the defeat of terrorism central to her policy in Northern Ireland.

Her years in office were shaped by violence. On 27 August 1979 the IRA killed Lord Mountbatten at Mullaghmore, Co. Sligo, and on the same day the Warrenpoint ambush killed eighteen soldiers. Later came the hunger strikes and the Brighton bombing.
She refused to grant political status to the hunger strikers, saying 'crime is crime is crime', and her government held firm during the 1981 protest.

She rejected the three options of the New Ireland Forum in November 1984, saying 'Out, out, out', yet in November 1985 she signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement with the Taoiseach Garret FitzGerald at Hillsborough Castle.
She was personally involved in the negotiations with FitzGerald in 1984 and 1985, and she signed the Agreement despite strong opposition from unionists.

Contemporary unionists regarded her as having betrayed the Union, while nationalists and Dublin welcomed the Agreement as a sign of British recognition of an Irish interest. Republicans regarded her as intransigent over the hunger strikes.

Historians differ on her motives. Some stress the hope of improved security cooperation with Dublin, others the aim of undercutting Sinn Féin's growth after 1981, and others her relations with Dublin and Washington. The Agreement did not end the violence.
notes.tip: For this personality, marks go to what she did (hunger strikers, Forum rejection, the Agreement) with dates, and to how contemporaries and historians judged her.

notes.b: The Agreement gave the Republic a formal consultative role in Northern Ireland for the first time. It was the biggest British policy shift since Sunningdale (the 1973 power-sharing agreement), and it survived fierce opposition.
points: It was signed on 15 November 1985 at Hillsborough Castle by Margaret Thatcher and Garret FitzGerald.

Thatcher's motives included improving cross-border security and winning back nationalist support from Sinn Féin, which was growing after 1981. The Irish government wanted to protect the SDLP, and the Forum had also shown that Dublin wanted a role.

It set up an Intergovernmental Conference of ministers, with a permanent joint secretariat at Maryfield near Belfast. Through it the Irish government could put forward views on Northern Ireland, though its role was consultative only.

Article 1 affirmed that there would be no change in the status of Northern Ireland without the consent of a majority of its people. This was the consent principle, and it reassured unionists in theory.

Unionists responded with the slogan 'Ulster says No', a large rally at Belfast City Hall on 23 November 1985 and a day of action in March 1986. Fifteen unionist MPs resigned their Westminster seats in January 1986, forcing by-elections, but the Agreement remained in force.

Republicans rejected the Agreement because it left British jurisdiction in place, and Fianna Fáil under Charles Haughey opposed it in the Dáil. The SDLP welcomed it as a limited but real step towards Irish involvement.
It was the biggest British policy shift since Sunningdale, and it survived despite the unionist campaign.
notes.tip: For Ordinary Level, learn the date, the place (Hillsborough Castle), the signatories (Thatcher and FitzGerald), the Intergovernmental Conference and Maryfield. Maryfield is the secretariat, not Hillsborough. Do not confuse it with Sunningdale (1973).

notes.b: Molyneaux led the Ulster Unionist Party through the period of the Anglo-Irish Agreement and was the main voice of mainstream unionist opposition.
points: James Molyneaux was born in 1920 and was MP for South Antrim from 1970 and for Lagan Valley from 1983. He became leader of the Ulster Unionist Party in 1979 and led it until 1995.
He led mainstream unionist opposition to the Anglo-Irish Agreement, and he worked with Ian Paisley, the confrontational leader of the DUP, on the 'Ulster says No' campaign.

He took part in the unionist campaign of 1985 and 1986, which included the 'Ulster says No' rally at Belfast City Hall on 23 November 1985 and the resignation of fifteen unionist MPs from Westminster in January 1986.
He favoured the integration of Northern Ireland into the United Kingdom's system of government rather than devolution (a separate local parliament), because he believed the Union was safest that way.
He cultivated good relations with Conservative ministers in the 1990s, and John Major's government at times relied on Ulster Unionist votes at Westminster, which gave him influence.
Contemporaries valued his caution and his commitment to the Union, although some unionists felt he was too passive in opposing the Agreement.
Historians regard him as a steady, quiet leader of mainstream unionism who opposed the Agreement without the confrontational style of Paisley. His strategy of opposition did not stop the Agreement.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Molyneaux (UUP, cautious) with Paisley (DUP, confrontational). For marks, give his dates as leader (1979 to 1995) and his opposition to the Agreement.

notes.h: Key personality: John Hume (part 3, SDLP leader and the Hume–Adams talks)
notes.b: Hume led the SDLP from 1979 and became the leading constitutional nationalist voice. His dialogue with Sinn Féin reshaped the search for peace.
points: John Hume became leader of the SDLP in 1979 and was elected to the European Parliament the same year.
He supported the Anglo-Irish Agreement, arguing that it gave nationalists a role in Northern Ireland's government.

He described the conflict as a problem of three relationships: within Northern Ireland, between North and South and between Ireland and Britain. This is why he believed that no solution could come from one relationship alone.
He began the dialogue with Gerry Adams in 1988 and argued that the IRA campaign must end if nationalists were to achieve their goals by dialogue.
He took part in the Brooke–Mayhew talks of 1991 and 1992, such as the attempt to set up a new devolved settlement.
Contemporaries regarded him as a moderate and effective nationalist leader, while unionists criticised him for talking to Sinn Féin.

Historians credit him with shaping the nationalist case for a peace process based on consent and dialogue, because his work with Adams and with the Irish government influenced the Downing Street Declaration.
notes.tip: Marks go to what Hume did (SDLP leader, dialogue with Adams, the Declaration) and to the judgements of contemporaries and historians. Do not confuse Hume–Adams (SDLP and Sinn Féin) with Brooke–Mayhew (British government and constitutional parties).

notes.h: The broadcast ban and the Hume–Adams dialogue, 1988–1993
notes.b: By 1988 the governments and republicans were fighting a battle over opinion as well as a military one. At the same time, the leaders of constitutional nationalism and republicanism began to talk.
points: In October 1988 the Home Secretary, Douglas Hurd, banned the broadcast of the voices of Sinn Féin spokespeople and others. Broadcasters used actors' voices, and the ban ended in 1994.
The ban was a propaganda measure by the government, intended to deny republicans a public platform, so it shaped opinion against them.
The Hume–Adams dialogue began in 1988, when the SDLP leader and the Sinn Féin president held talks that were publicly acknowledged.
The talks were controversial, with unionists and some nationalists objecting to contact between the SDLP and Sinn Féin while the IRA campaign continued.
The dialogue resumed in 1991 and produced joint statements in 1993. Historians regard it as an important precursor to the peace process, though it did not end the IRA campaign in this period.
notes.tip: For propaganda questions, show who was trying to influence whom: the government with the ban, republicans with hunger strike publicity, and the Peace People with their appeal.

notes.b: The Enniskillen bombing of 1987 became one of the best-known atrocities of the Troubles. It increased pressure for peace and damaged the IRA's standing.
points: On 8 November 1987, Remembrance Sunday, an IRA bomb exploded at the war memorial in Enniskillen, County Fermanagh, killing eleven people.
The victims were mostly elderly civilians who had gathered for the ceremony. A twelfth person, Ronnie Hill, died in 2000 after a long coma.
The IRA said it had intended to attack soldiers, but it admitted that the bombing was an error, and the attack was widely condemned.
Gordon Wilson, whose daughter Marie was killed, said in a BBC interview 'I bear no ill will', and he called for an end to violence.
The bombing was condemned in Britain, in Ireland and in the United States, and it damaged the IRA's standing because the victims were mostly elderly civilians.
notes.tip: Say 'mostly elderly civilians', not that all the victims were civilians. Give the date (8 November 1987), the place, the eleven deaths, Gordon Wilson and the effects.

notes.b: After the Agreement, the British government tried to bring the constitutional parties together again. Peter Brooke started the process, and Patrick Mayhew continued it, but no settlement followed.
points: Peter Brooke, as Secretary of State, said in November 1990 that Britain had no selfish strategic or economic interest in Northern Ireland. This signalled that Britain would not stand in the way of an agreed outcome.

The Brooke initiative of 1991 and the Mayhew talks of 1992 brought the parties together in multi-party talks, such as the British government and the constitutional parties, so they were a different format from Hume–Adams.
The talks did not produce agreement, so no devolved government was restored.
notes.tip: Keep Brooke–Mayhew (British government and constitutional parties) separate from Hume–Adams (SDLP and Sinn Féin). Both failed to end the violence.

notes.b: After the failed talks and continued violence, the British and Irish prime ministers issued a joint statement of principles. It set out the principles on which later peace efforts were built.
points: The Downing Street Declaration was issued on 15 December 1993 by Prime Minister John Major and Taoiseach Albert Reynolds.

It said that the Irish people as a whole had the right to self-determination, which could be exercised by agreement between North and South. It also said that a united Ireland would require the consent of a majority in Northern Ireland.

It said that the British government had no selfish strategic or economic interest in Northern Ireland and would legislate for a united Ireland if a majority wished it. It invited republicans to renounce violence and join talks.
The Irish government committed itself to set up a Forum for Peace and Reconciliation, and to examine Articles 2 and 3 of its constitution (the articles that claimed the whole island).

Nationalists and the Dublin government welcomed it, while unionists denounced it as a sign that Britain was moving towards a united Ireland. Sinn Féin and the IRA considered it, and the IRA ceasefire came in 1994, which falls outside this subsection.
notes.tip: For short answers, give the date, Major and Reynolds, self-determination, the consent of a majority and 'no selfish strategic or economic interest'. Do not confuse it with the Anglo-Irish Agreement of 1985.

notes.h: Assessment: the search for a settlement, 1974–1993
notes.b: To judge these steps, weigh what each achieved against what it failed to do. The Agreement and the Declaration are the two main steps, and examiners reward answers that compare them.
points: Achievement: the Anglo-Irish Agreement gave the Irish government a formal consultative role in Northern Ireland's affairs, a larger role than Sunningdale had given it.
Achievement: the Downing Street Declaration set out principles of consent and self-determination that became the basis for later agreements.
Limit: between 1974 and 1993 no devolved government was restored, and Direct Rule remained the basis of British policy.
Limit: the Hume–Adams dialogue and the Brooke and Mayhew talks did not end the IRA campaign. Violence continued throughout the period, as Brighton and Enniskillen show.
Contemporary view: nationalists and the Irish government regarded the Anglo-Irish Agreement and the Declaration as steps towards justice and peace.
Contemporary view: unionists regarded the Agreement as an infringement of their constitutional rights and denounced the Declaration as a sign that Britain was moving towards a united Ireland.
Later view: historians regard the period as one in which the framework for peace was built gradually, through dialogue, agreements and the acceptance of consent as a principle.
notes.tip: A narrative with no judgement scores poorly. In a comparison, give date, signatories, terms and effect for each, then say which mattered more and why, with both achievements and limits.

keyTerms.definition: The government of Northern Ireland by Westminster through a Secretary of State, in place from 1972 apart from the brief executive of 1974, and the framework for policy from 1974 to 1993.
The use of violence against civilians and the state for political ends, which the British government sought to defeat through security policy and political negotiation.
A system of government in which unionists and nationalists share power, which British governments sought but failed to restore between 1974 and 1993.
Materials and messages used to shape public opinion, which the British government and republicans both used during the hunger strikes and the Anglo-Irish negotiations.
The 1985 agreement between Thatcher and FitzGerald that gave the Irish government a consultative role in Northern Ireland through an Intergovernmental Conference.
The 15 December 1993 declaration by Major and Reynolds that accepted the principle of self-determination and majority consent for any change in Northern Ireland's status.
The policy from 1976 of transferring the security role of the British army to the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
A refusal of food by prisoners to press for political status, which in 1981 led to ten deaths including Bobby Sands.
The policy from 1976 of treating paramilitary prisoners as ordinary criminals and ending special category status.
The movement founded in August 1976 by Betty Williams and Mairead Corrigan after the deaths of three children in Belfast.
The 1983 to 1984 Dublin conference of the main nationalist parties, whose report offered three options for Irish unity that Thatcher rejected.
The principle that Northern Ireland's constitutional status could change only with the agreement of a majority of its people, restated in 1973, 1985 and 1993.
